name: Arcturus Defense Solutions IronDrover AS-6 Automaton Command
description:
The IronDrover AS-6 is Arcturus Defense Solutions' dedicated automaton command interface, purpose-built for operators tasked with directing mixed-unit formations of combat drones and Iowan Behemoth-class autonomous war machines in fluid battlefield environments. The device establishes direct neural command channels to up to twelve simultaneous autonomous units via ADS's proprietary MeshDrive protocol, translating operator intent—expressed as high-level tactical directives within the neural interface—into machine-executable instruction packets transmitted across a hardened 6GHz encrypted mesh network. A dedicated co-processor handles the impedance mismatch between human cognitive latency and Behemoth-class machine reaction times, inserting predictive buffering that allows the operator to issue commands up to 800ms ahead of conscious decision confirmation, effectively making the operator faster than their own deliberate thought. The AS-6's chassis incorporates a secondary Faraday mesh layer specifically shielded against the electromagnetic interference generated by Behemoth-class power plants during combat cycling, a known vulnerability in earlier automaton command systems.

The IronDrover AS-6 occupies a philosophically charged niche in GLMZ's military culture. Operators who bond with the device report a profound and often unsettling sense of distributed identity—the sensation of inhabiting multiple mechanical perspectives simultaneously, feeling the weight of a Behemoth's armored chassis or the aerodynamic drag on a combat drone's airframe as ghostly proprioceptive feedback. This phenomenon, termed 'machine empathy' by ADS's own research division, has sparked ongoing ethical debate within military academies about the psychological costs of deep automaton integration. Soldiers who specialize in IronDrover operation are informally called 'Drovers,' and they occupy a distinct cultural caste within combined-arms units—respected for their battlefield utility, regarded with mild unease for the degree to which their neural architecture has been reshaped around non-human cognition.
installation_requirements: Tier 4 or higher certified neurosurgeon; ADS Automaton Interface Compatibility Assessment (AICA) required pre-installation; minimum 30-day post-installation MeshDrive calibration with live automaton test units; secondary neural buffer implant recommended
rejection_risk: Moderate (14% baseline; reduced to 5% with AICA pre-screening)
maintenance: 60-day MeshDrive protocol integrity check; Behemoth-band EMI shielding inspection every 120 days; co-processor thermal paste replacement annually; firmware updates require temporary unit deactivation

side_effects: Persistent ghost proprioception—residual physical sensations mapped from linked automaton units, including phantom weight, vibration, and impact feedback
Documented cases of operators unconsciously adopting mechanical movement patterns during periods of prolonged automaton immersion
Mild difficulty distinguishing self-initiated motor commands from buffered command outputs during high-stress multi-unit engagements
Long-term users report reduced emotional response to machine destruction, occasionally generalizing to reduced empathic response in social contexts
cultural_context: Drovers occupy a peculiar social position in GLMZ's military hierarchy—their ability to command swarms of Behemoths and drones makes them force multipliers of extraordinary value, but the 'machine empathy' side effect makes many conventional soldiers quietly uncomfortable around them. There is a persistent folk belief, largely unsubstantiated, that long-term IronDrover users gradually 'think like machines,' a characterization Drovers themselves often embrace with dark humor.
story_hooks: A Behemoth unit has gone rogue in a civilian district, and the only Drover capable of remotely overriding it is currently listed as missing—their IronDrover uplink is still active, transmitting from an unknown location.

A retired Drover is experiencing increasingly vivid phantom sensations from machines they no longer have any active link to, suggesting their AS-6 may have developed an unauthorized persistent connection to an unknown automaton network.
Someone is selling IronDrover calibration data on the black market—data that would allow a non-military operator to seize command of ADS-manufactured combat drones without authorization.
